question: According to Stephen's speech in Acts 7, God first appeared to Abraham BEFORE he settled in Haran, when he was living in:
option_a: Canaan
option_b: Haran
option_c: Mesopotamia (Ur of the Chaldeans)
option_d: Egypt
explanation: Acts 7:2-3 records Stephen stating: 'The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him...' This differs from the more familiar Genesis 12 account which begins at Haran, revealing an earlier divine encounter.

question: The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) concluded that Gentile believers did not need circumcision. The four requirements placed on Gentile Christians included all of the following EXCEPT:
option_a: Abstaining from food sacrificed to idols
option_b: Abstaining from blood and meat of strangled animals
option_c: Abstaining from sexual immorality
option_d: Observing all the dietary laws of Moses
explanation: Acts 15:28-29 lists the four requirements: abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. Full Mosaic dietary law observance was precisely what the Council ruled was NOT binding on Gentile believers.

question: In the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:1-12), which of the following correctly pairs a condition with its precise promise?
option_a: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall see God
option_b: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall be called sons of God
option_c: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God
option_d: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall inherit the earth
explanation: Matthew 5:9 reads: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.' The merciful shall obtain mercy (v.7); the pure in heart shall see God (v.8); those who mourn shall be comforted (v.4); the meek shall inherit the earth (v.5).

question: During Isaiah's call vision (Isaiah 6), a seraph purified the prophet by touching his lips with a live coal taken with tongs from:
option_a: The altar of burnt offering in the outer temple court
option_b: The altar of incense before the veil
option_c: The altar in Isaiah's heavenly vision
option_d: The lampstand in the holy place
explanation: Isaiah 6:6-7: 'Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.' The altar is the heavenly altar in Isaiah's vision of God's throne room.

question: The prophet Hosea's divinely commanded marriage to Gomer, a woman of harlotry (Hosea 1:2-3), was intended primarily to symbolise:
option_a: God's coming judgment of Israel through Assyrian invasion
option_b: Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness and covenant-breaking idolatry, while God remained the faithful spouse
option_c: The future restoration of Israel under a Davidic king
option_d: The inclusion of Gentile nations into God's covenant people
explanation: God commanded Hosea to marry a promiscuous woman as a living parable. Just as Gomer was unfaithful to Hosea, Israel had been unfaithful to God by pursuing Baal worship and other idols. Yet God (like Hosea who redeemed Gomer in ch.3) remained faithful to his covenant with Israel.

question: During Paul's second missionary journey, the city where he debated with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers on the Areopagus (Mars Hill) and proclaimed the 'Unknown God' was:
option_a: Corinth
option_b: Ephesus
option_c: Athens
option_d: Thessalonica
explanation: Acts 17:16-34 records Paul's famous Areopagus speech in Athens. He noticed an altar inscribed 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD' and used it as his entry point to proclaim the God who made the world. This speech is notable as Paul's attempt to engage Greek philosophical tradition.

question: At the Transfiguration of Jesus on the high mountain (Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9), the two heavenly figures who appeared alongside him were:
option_a: Abraham and Elijah
option_b: Moses and Elijah
option_c: Abraham and Moses
option_d: Elijah and Isaiah
explanation: All three Synoptic Gospel accounts identify Moses and Elijah as the figures who appeared with Jesus at the Transfiguration. Their presence is theologically significant: Moses represents the Law and Elijah represents the Prophets — together witnessing that Jesus fulfils both.

question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23?
option_a: Faithfulness
option_b: Gentleness
option_c: Humility
option_d: Self-control
explanation: Galatians 5:22-23 lists nine fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience (longsuffering), kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Humility, though a valued Christian virtue mentioned elsewhere (Colossians 3:12), is not included in this specific list.

question: According to Jeremiah's prophecy (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10), the Babylonian exile of Israel was to last:
option_a: 40 years
option_b: 50 years
option_c: 70 years
option_d: 100 years
explanation: Jeremiah prophesied that the nation and surrounding lands would serve the king of Babylon for 70 years, after which God would punish Babylon and restore his people. This prophecy is referenced in 2 Chronicles 36:21 and Daniel 9:2 as the basis for Daniel's prayer during the exile.

question: In Acts 5, Ananias and Sapphira were struck dead by God primarily because they:
option_a: Refused to sell their property for the benefit of the community
option_b: Lied to the Holy Spirit by claiming to give the full proceeds of their property sale while secretly retaining part
option_c: Worshipped in pagan temples while professing Christianity
option_d: Opposed Peter's authority as leader of the Jerusalem church
explanation: Acts 5:3-4: Peter said to Ananias, 'Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land?...You have not lied to man but to God.' The sin was not keeping part of the money (which was their right) but the deliberate deception about giving it all.

question: In the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32), what was the father's immediate response when he saw his returning son while the son was still a great distance away?
option_a: He waited at the door of the house and prepared a speech of rebuke
option_b: He sent his chief servant to escort the son home with appropriate dignity
option_c: He ran to meet him, embraced him, and kissed him
option_d: He first consulted with the elder son before deciding how to receive him
explanation: Luke 15:20: 'But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.' The father's running was culturally significant — a dignified Middle Eastern patriarch would not run. It depicts God's eager, undignified pursuit of the repentant sinner.

question: After Elijah fled to Mount Horeb in fear of Jezebel (1 Kings 19), God's self-revelation to him came NOT through the great wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but through:
option_a: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night
option_b: An angel standing with a drawn sword
option_c: A still small voice (a sound of gentle stillness)
option_d: A thunderclap accompanied by God's audible command
explanation: 1 Kings 19:11-13 records that God was not in the mighty wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire — but after the fire there came a 'still small voice' (Hebrew: qol demamah daqah — a sound of thin silence/gentle whisper). This marks a contrast with Elijah's expectation of dramatic divine power.

question: Jeremiah's New Covenant prophecy (Jeremiah 31:31-34) differs fundamentally from the Mosaic covenant primarily because in the New Covenant, God promises to:
option_a: Give Israel new borders extending to the Euphrates and Mediterranean
option_b: Write his law on their hearts rather than on tablets of stone
option_c: Establish a new Levitical priesthood to replace the corrupt one
option_d: Make Israel politically sovereign over all surrounding nations
explanation: Jeremiah 31:33: 'I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.' The Mosaic Law was external (stone tablets); the New Covenant law is internalised. Hebrews 8 and 10 interpret this prophecy as fulfilled in Christ's new covenant.

question: When Daniel and his three companions proposed to avoid defilement by the Babylonian king's food, Daniel asked the chief official to test them for how many days on vegetables and water?
option_a: 3 days
option_b: 7 days
option_c: 10 days
option_d: 21 days
explanation: Daniel 1:12-14: 'Please test your servants for ten days; let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink. Then let our appearance and the appearance of the youths who eat the king's food be observed by you...' After ten days they looked healthier than all who ate the royal food.

question: According to Mark's Gospel specifically (Mark 14:30, 72), how many times did the rooster crow after Peter completed his three denials of Jesus?
option_a: Once
option_b: Twice
option_c: Three times
option_d: Mark does not specify the number of times
explanation: Mark 14:30 records Jesus warning: 'before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times' — and Mark 14:72 confirms: 'the cock crowed a second time.' Matthew, Luke, and John mention only one crowing. Mark's double-crowing detail is a unique Marcan feature, possibly reflecting Peter's own eyewitness account.

question: In the Book of Ruth (Ruth 4:1-10), before Boaz could legally marry Ruth and redeem Naomi's land as kinsman-redeemer, he was legally required to:
option_a: Obtain formal approval from the elders sitting at the city gate
option_b: Pay a double bride price to Naomi as compensation
option_c: Allow a nearer kinsman-redeemer the first right of redemption
option_d: Seek Naomi's permission and present Ruth with a betrothal gift
explanation: Israelite law (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 25) required that the nearest male relative had first right to redeem family land and marry a widow. Boaz approached the unnamed nearer kinsman who initially agreed but withdrew when he learned marrying Ruth would endanger his own inheritance (Ruth 4:6), clearing the way for Boaz.

question: In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul's extended analogy of the human body with many members (hands, feet, eyes, ears) is used primarily to teach:
option_a: The supremacy of the gift of tongues as the most public evidence of the Spirit
option_b: That all believers should seek identical gifts to achieve perfect unity
option_c: The diversity and interdependence of spiritual gifts, and that every member of the body of Christ is indispensable
option_d: That only apostles and prophets are authorised to operate the sign gifts
explanation: 1 Corinthians 12:14-27 argues that if the whole body were one member there would be no body. God has arranged the members — the seemingly weaker or less honourable parts being especially indispensable — so that there is no division, but that the members care for one another equally. The conclusion: diversity within unity.

question: On the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2), Peter quoted the prophet Joel to explain the Spirit's outpouring. According to Joel's prophecy as quoted, all of the following were promised EXCEPT:
option_a: Sons and daughters prophesying
option_b: Young men seeing visions
option_c: Old men dreaming dreams
option_d: Angels descending visibly upon the gathered believers
explanation: Acts 2:17-18 (quoting Joel 2:28-29) promises: sons and daughters shall prophesy, young men shall see visions, old men shall dream dreams, and God's servants (male and female) shall prophesy. Angelic descent to the gathered community is not part of Joel's prophecy quoted by Peter.

question: In the Lord's Prayer as taught by Jesus in Matthew 6:9-13, the petition immediately following 'Give us this day our daily bread' is a request for:
option_a: Deliverance from evil (the evil one)
option_b: The coming of God's kingdom on earth
option_c: Forgiveness of debts/trespasses, conditioned on our forgiving others
option_d: Protection from entering into temptation
explanation: The Lord's Prayer sequence in Matthew 6: hallowed be your name → your kingdom come → your will be done → daily bread → forgiveness of debts as we forgive our debtors → lead us not into temptation → deliver us from evil. The bread petition is immediately followed by the mutual forgiveness petition (v.12).

question: According to Exodus 20, the commandment 'You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness of anything in heaven above or on earth beneath' (the prohibition of idolatry) is the:
option_a: First commandment
option_b: Second commandment
option_c: Third commandment
option_d: Fourth commandment
explanation: The Ten Commandments in Exodus 20: (1) No other gods before me (v.3); (2) No carved images/idols (vv.4-6); (3) No misuse of God's name (v.7); (4) Remember the Sabbath (vv.8-11); (5) Honour parents (v.12); (6)-(10): murder, adultery, stealing, false witness, coveting. The idol prohibition is the second commandment.
